title: POC Weekly Caching Sync - Prefix/KV hit rate review
summary: Weekly POC sync to review cache hit-rate improvements after prefix normalization and TTL tuning. Team saw prefix hit rate increase from ~38% to ~61% in best buckets; KV hit rate improvements modest due to prompt variability. Discussed canonicalization, deduping, and rollout strategy; security/retention questions from Priya. Agreed actions: share dashboard, run 100k prompt benchmark, update caching config and TTL, schedule security checklist meeting.
transcript:
Header: Date/Time: 2026-08-11 10:00 PDT | Duration 45m
Attendees: Alice Park (Redwood AE), Ben Cho (Redwood SE), Sarah Kim (Lumina Head of ML), Mike Ortega (Lumina Infra), Priya Desai (Lumina Security), Jamal Reed (Lumina PM)
----
[00:00] Alice Park: hey everyone, thanks for joining the weekly caching sync, uh we have the usual agenda — quick results, tuning notes, and next steps. Ben's going to walk through the dashboard.
[00:32] Ben Cho: cool, hi all. I pulled the numbers from the last 7 days after we applied the prefix normalization and the TTL changes. overall prefix hit rate, so this is the short prompt prefix grouping, went from about thirty eight percent up to roughly sixty one percent in the user-question bucket — so that's a decent uplift. KV cache hit rate improved less, from about 12% to 18% in aggregate.
[01:05] Sarah Kim: can you clarify prefix vs KV here? sometimes folks on my team conflate them.
[01:15] Ben Cho: sure, prefix cache is keyed on the initial prompt tokens or canonicalized prompt head — it's faster to hit for repeated question stems. KV cache is the model's kv cache reuse across continuation tokens; it helps when sessions have similar latent states. the two are complementary.
[01:40] Mike Ortega: so the 61% is only for the subset of calls that match our canonicalization rules right? like if users include dynamic context we still miss a lot.
[01:50] Ben Cho: correct — we see the biggest gains when prompts are normalized — removing timestamps, normalizing names, replacing UUIDs with placeholders. for flows where the PM injects a fresh conversation state per request, prefix hits are lower.
[02:10] Jamal Reed: we did add prompt templating on the frontend for the top 10 intents which helped. are those the buckets you measured?
[02:18] Ben Cho: yes we prioritized the top 10 intents; those saw the largest hit-rate improvements. overall distribution: top intent bucket hit rate now ~71%, tail intents still low ~22%.
[02:33] Priya Desai: quick security question — where is the cached data stored and what's the retention window? we need to show this to compliance.
[02:42] Alice Park: good call, Priya. for the POC we used Redwood-hosted ephemeral cache with encryption-at-rest. TTLs are set to 24 hours by default but we lowered some to 3 hours for sensitive routes. we can provide the audit log extract.
[03:02] Priya Desai: can you add the KMS key id and the retention policy to the doc? also need to confirm whether cache keys contain any PII — if yes we have to hash or redact.
[03:14] Ben Cho: yeah, we recommend hashing identifiers; we showed a sample redaction pipeline last week. I'll add the exact key IDs to the security doc and drop it into the shared drive.
[03:29] Sarah Kim: back to hit rates — any idea why KV didn't improve as much? I'd expected larger gains since many sessions reuse similar sequences.
[03:38] Ben Cho: two reasons: first, KV benefit depends on sequence alignment and checkpointing. second, we observed a lot of micro-variations in follow-up prompts — small paraphrases break exact matches. we're testing fuzzy keying via n-gram hashing and also trying a TTL-based sticky window to keep KV for slightly longer for repeat users.
[04:00] Alice Park: we also ran an experiment with canonicalization of trailing system messages which gave a modest KV lift. Ben, did you have the latency numbers?
[04:10] Ben Cho: yes. median latency for cached hits (prefix or KV) is ~85 ms, non-cache median is ~240 ms. cost per successful cached request falls dramatically as you avoid full decode. but there's a small tail latency risk when cache lookup adds overhead on top of routing, roughly +10ms 95th percentile. overall tradeoff is favorable.
[04:35] Mike Ortega: what's the memory footprint on the node for the cache? we have constrained instance sizes for the on-prem evaluation.
[04:44] Ben Cho: current config for the POC uses about 12GB of RAM per shard for the KV store with an LRU of 2M entries; we can down-sample keys and use bloom filters to reduce memory at a small hit-rate cost.
[05:02] Sarah Kim: did you try deduping prompts at ingestion? that could boost KV hits.
[05:08] Ben Cho: we did dedupe by prompt hash, but hash collisions and natural paraphrases made strict dedupe brittle. so we moved to a two-tier approach: strict hash dedupe for exact repeats and fuzzy cluster for near-duplicates, which increases compute but helps KV hit rate.
[05:28] Jamal Reed: how much extra compute are we talking about? our cost targets are tight.
[05:32] Ben Cho: fuzzy clustering uses a lightweight n-gram sketch; in our test environment it added about 5% CPU per request at peak. cost tradeoff depends on how much cache hit rate you recover — for top intents it's worthwhile.
[05:48] Sarah Kim: numbers on cost savings?
[05:50] Ben Cho: rough estimate: with current 61% prefix hit and 18% KV, effective full-model calls are down about 55%, which reduced tokens billed by about 52% on the POC workload. we can send the detailed cost spreadsheet.
[06:10] Alice Park: action item — Ben to share the cost workbook and dashboard link.
[06:14] Ben Cho: noted. I'll post the dashboard and cost sheet after this call.
[06:20] Priya Desai: regarding privacy again — can we get an automated scan to ensure keys don't embed raw emails or SSNs?
[06:27] Ben Cho: yes we have a scrubber that runs at ingestion; it's configured in the pipeline but we need to show logs. I'll export sample scrubber logs for you.
[06:37] Mike Ortega: on TTL tuning, you said some routes switched from 24h to 3h. which routes and why?
[06:45] Ben Cho: authentication and claim-detail routes were shortened due to PII; product search remained at 24h to preserve UX. We can publish a route table.
[06:56] Sarah Kim: longer term — would you recommend client-side prompt canonicalization or server-side?
[07:03] Ben Cho: both. client-side is cheapest because it reduces network payload and obvious noise; server-side canonicalization is a safety net for third-party integrations. For Lumina we recommend enforcing templates in the client for top intents and server-side canonicalization for the rest.
[07:20] Jamal Reed: timeline for rolling client changes? our dev sprint can push templating next week.
[07:25] Alice Park: that's great — if you push templates we'll re-run the 100k prompt benchmark.
[07:30] Ben Cho: speaking of benchmarks, we picked a sample of 100k prompts from production logs, shuffled, and ran a daytime/peak split. after canonicalization the expected hit-rate projection is 65-70% for head intents. we can run the full job this week.
[07:50] Mike Ortega: is this going to be disruptive? we can't spike infra costs to run big tests.
[07:55] Ben Cho: we'll run the benchmark on Redwood staging with rate-limited traffic; it shouldn't be resource-prohibitive.
[08:02] Alice Park: Priya, do you want security in the benchmark run? e.g., to assert that scrubber removed PII?
[08:08] Priya Desai: yes please add me to the run so we can sample outputs.
[08:13] Ben Cho: will do.
[08:16] Sarah Kim: you mentioned fuzzy keying — any false positives that could return wrong content?
[08:22] Ben Cho: fuzzy keying is conservative; if similarity is above threshold we may serve cached completions that are near-suitable. for safety-critical routes we avoid fuzzy keys. we'll keep those disabled for claim processing.
[08:37] Jamal Reed: ok, next on the list: eviction strategy — LRU currently, but we discussed age-based tiers?
[08:44] Ben Cho: right, we propose a hybrid: LRU for general routes, TTL-first for sensitive routes, and a hot-set tier for the top intents which is pinned with longer TTL and more memory. that gave us the best hit-rate/cost mix in staging.
[09:00] Mike Ortega: are there any integration changes for Dedicated or Private deployment? we may want to test on our on-prem cluster.
[09:08] Alice Park: for Private we'd package the cache as a local service with the same API; mem footprint and encryption configs will be adjustable. Ben, can we create an on-prem config with 8GB footprint?
[09:18] Ben Cho: yes — we'll provide a low-memory profile, remove the hot-set pinning by default, and add bloom filters to reduce keys. performance will be slightly lower but predictable.
[09:30] Sarah Kim: what's the expected hit-rate drop in low-memory profile?
[09:33] Ben Cho: ~6-9 percentage points on prefix hit in our tests, depends on traffic distribution.
[09:40] Priya Desai: one more security item — audit logs must show cache lookup events and key hashes. can you expose that?
[09:48] Ben Cho: yes, we have lookup events and can surface hashed keys and TTL decisions. I'll add that to the security artifact.
[09:58] Alice Park: alright let's recap and assign next steps.
[10:02] Ben Cho: recap: share dashboard + cost sheet, run 100k benchmark, export scrubber logs, produce on-prem low-memory config, and add audit log extract.
[10:12] Jamal Reed: agree. timeline?
[10:15] Ben Cho: dashboard and cost sheet today; scrubber logs and audit extract by Thursday; benchmark run Friday; on-prem config early next week.
[10:24] Priya Desai: please cc security on all artifacts.
[10:27] Alice Park: will do. thanks all. we'll follow up in the Loom and in the shared drive.
[10:34] Meeting end: quick check — any other questions? (no) thanks everyone.
----
